summary: Describes practices for operating DNS with security extensions, aimed at zone administrators deploying DNSSEC. It covers key generation, key storage, signature generation, key rollover, and related issues. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6781 describes operational decisions for administrators of DNSSEC-signed zones. It explains how key roles, signature timing, and cached records affect rollovers and validation.

questions: best practices for dnssec zone administrators
what is a ksk and zsk
subtitle: Operational choices for signing DNS zones, handling keys, and keeping validation working.

tldr.problem: Signing a DNS zone is not enough: keys, signatures, caches, and parent-zone records must remain coordinated during normal operation and changes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC discusses key roles and storage, key and algorithm rollovers, timing, parent policies, and authenticated denial of nonexistent names.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6781 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 4641. The authors say it is not Best Current Practices and give no strong recommendations.

today: RFC 6781 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 4641. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the RFC says it is not Best Current Practices.

sections.title: Keeping the Chain of Trust Working
sections.content:
The RFC is for people who operate authoritative DNS zones and want to deploy DNSSEC. It discusses decisions and available choices rather than prescribing one operational method. The authors explicitly say the document should not be treated as Best Current Practices.

A broken chain of trust can cause signed data to be marked Bogus and make a domain unavailable to validating clients. Changes also take time to reach secondary servers and to replace data held in caches, so signing and rollover plans must account for propagation and timing.
sections.plainLanguage: DNSSEC validation depends on a chain of records and signatures linking a zone to a trust anchor. A change must account for old information that may still be cached.

sections.title: Key Roles, Storage, and Lifetime
sections.content:
A Key Signing Key (KSK) signs the zone's DNSKEY set at the apex. A Zone Signing Key (ZSK) signs other zone data. This split is an operational choice; DNSSEC validators do not treat the key types differently. A ZSK can be replaced without parent interaction, while changing a KSK may require a new DS record at the parent or updates to configured trust anchors.

The RFC discusses keeping private keys and the master zone file on offline, physically secure systems where practical. Dynamic updates may require a private key on the master server or in an accessible hardware security module. It describes about one year as a reasonable effectivity period for a regularly rolled KSK with a parent and about a month for an online ZSK with higher exposure, while noting that there is no widespread agreement on rollover policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators may use one key for all signing or separate keys for the DNSKEY set and other records. Separate keys allow a zone-signing key to be changed without asking the parent to update its record.

sections.title: Rolling or Replacing Keys
sections.content:
Resolvers may cache old keys, signatures, or zone data during a rollover. If a cached signature cannot be checked with a key available to the resolver, the data may be marked Bogus. For a ZSK, Pre-Publish introduces the new key before using it and takes four stages; Double-Signature signs data with both keys during the overlap and takes three stages.

Pre-Publish avoids doubling signatures but publishes the new public key before use. Double-Signature uses more signatures during the transition. KSK changes also require parent coordination and waiting for cached DS records to expire. The RFC discusses emergency replacement and says a compromised KSK should not be removed before the parent has a DS record for its replacement.
sections.plainLanguage: Publish replacement keys early enough for cached data to remain verifiable during a change. KSK changes also involve the parent zone, so they require coordination and additional waiting.

sections.title: Parent Records and Signature Timing
sections.content:
A DS record at the parent points to a child-zone DNSKEY. Security lameness occurs when the parent has a DS record pointing to a DNSKEY that does not exist. During a Double-DS rollover this may happen temporarily, but if all DS records point nowhere, validating clients mark the child zone Bogus. The RFC suggests that a DS signature validity period could be between a week and several months.

DNSSEC signatures use absolute expiration times, while DNS data may remain in caches. The RFC suggests keeping the maximum zone TTL below the signature validity period and refreshing signatures before they approach expiration. It also suggests an SOA expiration timer of about one third or one quarter of that validity period.
sections.plainLanguage: Parent DS records and child DNSKEY records must refer to one another during a rollover. Signatures also need refreshing before they expire, while cached data may still be in use.

sections.title: Choosing NSEC or NSEC3
sections.content:
NSEC and NSEC3 provide signed evidence that a DNS name does not exist. NSEC lists names in sorted order in clear text. NSEC3 hashes the names before creating a sorted list, which makes enumeration harder but does not hide the zone's size or the record types it contains.

The RFC prefers NSEC for highly structured zones or small zones with easily guessed names. It prefers NSEC3 for large zones where names are not meant to be readily available. NSEC3 iterations increase the work of dictionary attacks but also increase signing and validation costs; the RFC considers 100 iterations costly but not excessive. Opt-Out is intended for zones with many insecure delegations.
sections.plainLanguage: NSEC exposes the ordered names in a zone, while NSEC3 hashes them before listing them. Hashing makes enumeration harder, but it does not conceal every fact about the zone.

sections.title: Security Limits and Operational Risk
sections.content:
DNSSEC provides data-origin authentication and data integrity using digital signatures. It does not provide confidentiality or protection against denial-of-service attacks.

The operational risk emphasized by this RFC is failure during key or signature changes. Cached data may no longer match the authoritative zone, causing validation failures and making the secured zone unavailable to security-aware resolvers.
sections.plainLanguage: DNSSEC helps validators check who signed DNS data and whether it changed. It does not hide the data or prevent denial-of-service attacks, and careless rollovers can break validation.
